items.title: Web CSP allows script-src 'unsafe-inline'
items.userProblem: The signed-in web surface permits inline script execution, weakening the main defence against XSS becoming session theft.
items.source: Forensic security audit finding M-2, 2026-09-25 - VERIFIED by the Orchestrator
acceptanceCriteria: script-src 'unsafe-inline' is removed from the web Content-Security-Policy, or retained with a documented, specific reason and a recorded compensating control
Any nonce or hash strategy works with the Next.js App Router in production, not only in development
The change is proven by a real browser run, not asserted - the repaired cross-engine suite can enforce it
evidence: VERIFIED BY THE ORCHESTRATOR 2026-09-25 against current bytes, settling a claim the auditor explicitly could NOT confirm (it had no shell and was carrying it forward rather than asserting it). v2/apps/web/next.config.ts line 27 reads: "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; ". The finding is TRUE.
DO NOT CONFLATE THE TWO SURFACES: the API-side CSP is strict and correct - helmet with default-src 'none' and frame-ancestors 'none'. This finding is about the WEB surface only.

CONTEXT that bounds the severity: docs/KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md already discloses "unsafe-inline styles/scripts remain in CSP" as a residual risk in its threat table, so this is a known, disclosed gap rather than a new discovery. style-src 'unsafe-inline' is substantially harder to remove than script-src and may legitimately remain.

FIXED PROPERLY 2026-09-25 rather than documented-and-accepted, which AC1 also permitted. The blocker was structural: next.config.ts headers() is STATIC, evaluated once at build time, so it cannot emit the per-request value a nonce needs. Added v2/apps/web/src/middleware.ts (there was no middleware in this app before) generating a per-request nonce and setting script-src 'self' 'nonce-<n>' 'strict-dynamic'. The CSP moved out of next.config entirely so there is ONE place a reader must look - two copies of a security policy is how one of them silently drifts. A nonce was chosen over hashes because the App Router emits inline bootstrap and flight-data scripts whose content changes per route and per build; a hash allowlist would need regenerating on every change and would break silently the moment one was missed. 'self' is kept alongside 'strict-dynamic' as the fallback for browsers that do not implement CSP Level 3 - they ignore strict-dynamic and fall back to the host source, still far stronger than 'unsafe-inline'. style-src 'unsafe-inline' is DELIBERATELY RETAINED and recorded as an accepted residual: AC1 is written about script-src, inline styles are a materially smaller risk, and removing them would require nonce-ing every style Next and the component tree emit. Not silently carried - stated in the file and here.

AC3 ("proven by a real browser run, not asserted") SATISFIED. Added an assertion to v2/scripts/check-ui.ts against the REAL DOCUMENT RESPONSE HEADER, not the config file, because the header is what a browser enforces and the config is only one of the places it could come from. IT IS A POSITIVE AND A NEGATIVE ASSERTION ON PURPOSE, and the reason is subtle enough to record: proving a nonce is present would NOT prove 'unsafe-inline' had gone, and a browser IGNORES 'unsafe-inline' whenever a nonce is present - so a policy carrying both would look like it worked while leaving the weaker token in place for any CSP Level 2 browser. The check asserts the directive exists, that it does NOT contain 'unsafe-inline', and that it DOES carry a nonce. VERIFIED: live header on / reads "script-src 'self' 'nonce-YmY3...' 'strict-dynamic'" with no unsafe-inline. Full check-ui suite exit 0 on chromium, firefox and webkit - which is the real proof the app still hydrates, since a nonce mistake breaks every inline script and the suite exercises every route. v2 typecheck 0. VERIFICATION LEVEL: LOCALLY VERIFIED against the dev server. NOT verified against a production build, and NOT CI-EXECUTED.

REVIEWER REJECTED PROMOTION ON AC2 AND WAS EXACTLY RIGHT. AC2 says the strategy must work "with the Next.js App Router in production, not only in development", and my own evidence closed with "LOCALLY VERIFIED against the dev server. NOT verified against a production build." Those two sentences contradicted each other, and the reviewer named the mechanism precisely: statically prerendered HTML is generated at BUILD time and cannot carry a per-request nonce. It asked me to run the production build before anything else. I did, and it broke.

MEASURED FAILURE, NOT INFERRED - this is the durable content of this ticket. npm run build succeeded and listed the middleware as active. Against npm run start:web (a real production server, not the dev server): the response header DID advertise a nonce, but curl on / returned 10 <script> tags and ZERO nonce= attributes. Next did not stamp the nonce onto scripts it had already emitted at build time. Because strict-dynamic makes the nonce authoritative and causes 'self' to be ignored on any browser implementing CSP Level 3, none of those ten scripts could execute. npm run test:ui went RED against production - locator.boundingBox timed out because the page never hydrated. The dev server had passed every one of those assertions minutes earlier. This is precisely the gap AC2 exists to catch, and without the production run I would have shipped a CSP that silently bricks the deployed app.

REVERTED: src/middleware.ts deleted, the policy restored to next.config.ts with script-src unsafe-inline intact, dev server restored, test:ui exit 0 on chromium/firefox/webkit, lint 0, typecheck 0. The full reasoning is recorded in a comment in next.config.ts so the next person does not repeat the attempt blind. WHAT THE REAL FIX COSTS, now known rather than guessed: removing unsafe-inline requires either abandoning static prerendering (forcing dynamic rendering on every route) or moving to build-time hashes of Next own generated inline scripts. Both are genuine architectural decisions with performance and maintenance cost, and neither belongs inside a CSP ticket. This is no longer a header edit. COMPENSATING CONTROLS, verified present: session cookies are httpOnly so script cannot read them; sameSite strict; the API sets its own strict policy (default-src none); no dangerouslySetInnerHTML anywhere in the app; every rendered value goes through React automatic escaping.

F-2 WAS THE MOST IMPORTANT FINDING AND IS NOW MOOT BUT WORTH KEEPING: my nonce assertion (assert.match on /'nonce-[A-Za-z0-9+/=]+'/) would have passed happily against a CONSTANT nonce. Hoisting the crypto.randomUUID() line to module scope - a plausible optimisation - would have reduced the policy to an allowlist of one guessable value. A constant nonce is not a degraded CSP, it is a defeated one, and the entire suite would have stayed green. That is a FIFTH check-that-cannot-fail, and the first one caught BEFORE it shipped rather than after. I had implemented the two-request uniqueness assertion before the production run made the whole approach moot. F-3 and F-4 are moot with the middleware gone. F-5 SURVIVES AND WAS KEPT: check-ui.ts now parses the CSP into directives and asserts default-src, object-src, base-uri, frame-ancestors and form-action by EQUALITY rather than substring, so a widened or dropped directive fails. That is real coverage this ticket added and it stays, along with a loud failure when the header is absent entirely. The script-src unsafe-inline weakness is deliberately NOT asserted away - it stays open here.

MEASURED 2026-09-25 (orchestrator session, web tier), and it REVISES THE TICKETS OWN ASSUMPTION. The reverted-nonce comment in next.config.ts concluded that removing unsafe-inline "requires giving up static prerendering OR moving to build-time hashes". Measurement against the real production build shows the first half is unnecessary: ALL 13 app routes are prerendered and ZERO render per request, so every inline script IS known at build time. Static prerendering does NOT have to be abandoned.

THE NUMBERS, from v2/apps/web/.next, confirmed a genuine production build before being trusted (BUILD_ID, prerender-manifest.json, routes-manifest.json and required-server-files.json all present; no .next/static/development directory, so not a dev artefact): 13 prerendered HTML files, 26 inline <script> elements with a body, 0 carrying a nonce (consistent with the earlier measured failure), and only 12 DISTINCT sha256 hashes. One is the (self.__next_f=self.__next_f||[]).push([0]) bootstrap shared by all 13 pages; the rest are per-page Flight payloads. A hash policy needs 12 entries, not hundreds.

WHAT STILL BLOCKS IT IS ORDERING, NOT FEASIBILITY: headers() in next.config.ts is evaluated DURING the build, before the HTML containing those scripts exists, so the hashes cannot be computed and consumed in one pass. Same class of problem as the nonce - a static header trying to describe content it has not seen. Two workable shapes, both needing a BUILD PIPELINE change: a two-pass build (build, hash the emitted HTML, rebuild with headers() reading the generated file), or generating a hash manifest at build time and serving the policy at the edge.

ONE ASSUMPTION EXPLICITLY NOT VERIFIED, stated rather than glossed: the two-pass approach is only viable if the second pass emits BYTE-IDENTICAL HTML. That was not tested, because rebuilding would overwrite .next underneath a dev server running on 5280 that other sessions may be using. Recorded as unverified rather than assumed true.

TWO TRAPS RECORDED BEFORE ANYONE IMPLEMENTS IT. (1) A hash policy that is merely PRESENT proves nothing: asserting script-src contains "sha256-" would pass while unsafe-inline sits beside it - and unsafe-inline is IGNORED once hashes are present, so the policy would look strict, behave strictly, and the assertion would have measured neither. The assertion must be that unsafe-inline is ABSENT, paired with a positive that the page actually rendered. (2) The stale-hash failure is silent in CI and loud in production: if the pipeline forgets to regenerate the manifest the policy still parses and the site still returns 200, with nothing executing.

FAILURE MODE IS A BLANK PAGE, NOT A WEAKER POLICY - the same outcome as the reverted nonce. A single missing hash means React hydration and Flight payloads do not execute. So it must be proven the way the original failure was found: against a PRODUCTION server in a real browser, never against the dev server and never by reading the config.

SCOPE HELD UNDER THE THREE-SESSION PARTITION: the measurement, docs/CSP-STRICT-SCRIPT-SRC.md and the corrected next.config.ts comment are all in the web tier and docs, which this session owns. The IMPLEMENTATION is deliberately NOT started - a two-pass build touches build scripts and the edge option touches infrastructure, both of which belong to the infrastructure session. Handed off rather than half-done. CS-54 stays READY, not promoted; nothing here is CI-executed and the SHA has not moved.

DEMOTED FROM READY 2026-09-25 on independent audit, AND THE TICKET CONTRADICTED ITSELF IN A WAY A PICKER-UP WOULD NOT SEE. Its own final evidence says the implementation is deliberately not started and belongs to the infrastructure session - and it then left itself READY with ownerAgent: Frontend, architectureImpact "Next.js CSP/nonce strategy", no dependency recorded and no owner reassignment. Anyone picking it up as Frontend could not finish it. ownerAgent corrected to Infrastructure in this edit.

THE REMAINING IMPLEMENTATION PATH RESTS ON AN UNTESTED PREMISE, quoted from this ticket: "the two-pass approach is only viable if the second pass emits BYTE-IDENTICAL HTML. That was not tested." That is a DISCOVERY-grade unknown, not a READY task - if the HTML is not byte-identical the hashes are wrong, and the failure mode this ticket states twice is A BLANK PAGE, NOT A WEAKER POLICY. CS-61 needed an amendment; this needs an EXPERIMENT THAT MAY VOID ITS PLAN.

BUT THERE IS A LEGITIMATE SAME-DAY CLOSE NOBODY HAD NAMED, and it comes from reading AC1 cold: it is a DISJUNCTION - "script-src unsafe-inline is removed ... OR retained with a documented, specific reason and a recorded compensating control". BRANCH 2 IS ALREADY SATISFIED AT SOURCE. next.config.ts carries the measured reason (13 prerendered routes, 26 inline scripts, 12 distinct hashes, and the nonce attempts production failure) and enumerates verified compensating controls - httpOnly, sameSite strict, API default-src none, no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, React auto-escaping - with the residual already in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md.

STATUS CHOICE FLAGGED FOR OVERRIDE: the coordinator offered DISCOVERY or close-on-branch-2. This session chose BLOCKED because the deciding input is an OWNER BINARY, and the CS-30 lesson recorded hours earlier is precisely that a ticket waiting on the owner must appear in the BLOCKED column the owner reads - DISCOVERY would hide the cheapest security close on the board in the ideas column. If the coordinator prefers DISCOVERY it is a one-line change.

GENUINE WIN THAT SURVIVED THE REVERT, recorded so the ticket is not read as wholly negative: check-ui.ts now parses the CSP into directives and asserts default-src, object-src, base-uri, frame-ancestors and form-action BY EQUALITY, NOT SUBSTRING. That is permanent coverage this ticket added, independent of whether unsafe-inline is ever removed.
REVIEW WINDOW CAVEAT: three sessions were writing concurrently; re-check if a cited file moved between roughly 15:05 and 16:45 IST on 2026-09-25.

RUNTIME CAVEAT ADDED 2026-09-25 TO EVERY RESULT RECORDED TODAY: all local verification in this run was executed on Node v22.23.2, while package.json requires >=24.0.0, .nvmrc says 24 and CI uses 24. This does not invalidate the passes, but it RECLASSIFIES them - each was obtained on a runtime the project does not support, and any could differ on Node 24. Applies to typecheck, lint, test:unit, deploy:gate:test, eol:check and the three-engine test:ui runs alike.

STALE FIELD CORRECTED 2026-09-25, AND IT WAS THIS SESSIONS OWN: currentStep still opened "READY, reopened" while the status had been BLOCKED for over an hour. That is precisely the field-disagreement defect this session has corrected on CS-38, CS-50, CS-30 and CS-52 today, appearing on a ticket this session had itself demoted. The board renders currentStep, so a reader would have seen READY on a BLOCKED ticket.

THE LESSON IS NOT "BE MORE CAREFUL": it is that changing `status` and changing the fields that DESCRIBE the status are two separate acts, and nothing enforces that the second follows the first. CS-73 already proposes a validator for ownerAgent/architectureImpact consistency; currentStep-versus-status belongs in the same check.

PROVISIONAL MARKING WITHDRAWN 2026-09-25, SAME DAY IT WAS APPLIED, BECAUSE IT WAS TOO BROAD AND THE WITHDRAWAL IS RECORDED RATHER THAN SILENT. The #19 finding was real - tsc -b exited 0 with a production type error - BUT IT WAS OVERSTATED AS "the gate could not fail". THE GATE COULD FAIL; ONLY ITS FIRST LINK COULD NOT. `npm run typecheck` chains four commands and the last, check-test-types.mjs, filters on /^\S+\.ts\(\d+,\d+\): error TS\d+/ - WHICH MATCHES A PRODUCTION FILE AS READILY AS A TEST FILE - and exits 1. Anyone running the npm script WOULD have been told.

THIS TICKET DOES NOT CITE A BARE `tsc -b`, so its typecheck evidence was never in the unfalsifiable form and stands unqualified. The narrowed set is 4 of the original 29: CS-53, CS-62, CS-76, CS-77 - ALL FOUR WRITTEN BY THE ORCHESTRATOR, which is the correct place for the correction to land.

RE-CONFIRMED BLOCKED 2026-09-26 AND DELIBERATELY NOT ATTEMPTED. Branch 2 of the AC1 disjunction - retain unsafe-inline with a documented reason and a recorded compensating control - IS STILL SATISFIED AT SOURCE: next.config.ts carries "CS-54: script-src unsafe-inline is a real, disclosed weakness and it is STILL HERE - deliberately, with the reason measured rather than assumed", and the middleware history is recorded beside it.

NO WORK WAS ATTEMPTED THIS CYCLE, WHICH IS THE CORRECT OUTCOME RATHER THAN AN OMISSION. The remaining options are (a) close on branch 2, marking AC2 vacuous-and-disclosed, or (b) pursue branch 1, whose only surviving path rests on an UNTESTED byte-identical-HTML premise. BOTH ARE OWNER DECISIONS ABOUT ACCEPTED RISK, NOT ENGINEERING TASKS, so attempting either would be an agent deciding a security posture unilaterally.

AND THE PROHIBITION HOLDS AND IS RESTATED SO IT SURVIVES A FUTURE READER WITH FRESH ENTHUSIASM: DO NOT RETRY THE NONCE MIDDLEWARE. A production run already proved that route ships an application THAT DOES NOT LOAD. That is a stronger disqualification than a failing test, because it was observed against a real build rather than inferred.

items.title: Eleven authenticated GET routes have no rate limit, including the most expensive read, which the UI polls
items.userProblem: A single stuck browser tab becomes a sustained load generator against the most expensive unmetered endpoint in the application.
items.source: Forensic security audit finding M-3, 2026-09-25
acceptanceCriteria: Authenticated GET routes carry a proportionate rate limit, with the most expensive reads limited most strictly
Existing legitimate client polling continues to work and is not broken by the limit - the limit must be derived from the real polling intervals, not guessed
Limits are proven by test at both the allowed and the rejected boundary, never only the happy path
evidence: AUDIT FINDING M-3: eleven authenticated GET routes carry no rate limit. The most significant is GET /api/searches/:id, described as the most expensive read in the application - two 100-row JSONB queries plus a 100-row event scan, with every row re-parsed through Zod.

The client amplifies it: the Jobs page polls /api/searches/:id every 10 seconds while a run is active, and polls /api/searches every 5 seconds UNCONDITIONALLY. So the expensive endpoint is not merely unmetered, it is unmetered and continuously called by the product own UI.

Rate limiting demonstrably EXISTS and works in this codebase - POST /api/account/password and POST /api/account/sessions/revoke-others both carry a real 5/hour limit. So this is an inconsistent application of an existing control, not a missing capability.

NOT INDEPENDENTLY RE-VERIFIED by the Orchestrator in this cycle (route count and polling intervals carried forward from the audit). Confirm against v2/apps/api/src/app.ts and the web query configuration before implementing, and derive the limit from the real intervals.

MEASURED TESTING COST, 2026-09-25 - this finding no longer rests on reasoning alone. While writing the CS-36 cross-session test I used the suite own quiet() helper (waits until no non-streaming request has been in flight for 250ms) on /jobs and it FAILED: "chromium: cs-36 reset /jobs never stopped issuing requests". Cause is exactly this ticket finding: /jobs polls /api/searches every 5 seconds UNCONDITIONALLY, so the route can never reach a settled state. The unmetered polling therefore has a concrete, reproduced cost beyond the hypothetical availability one - it makes a real route structurally untestable by any settle-based technique, and forced the CS-36 test to use a different waiting strategy. That is a second, independent reason to fix it, and it is observable today rather than under load.

HALF THE OUTSTANDING DISCOVERY IS CLOSED 2026-09-25, recorded so whoever picks this up does not redo it. The blocker required confirming against app.ts AND the web query configuration. THE WEB HALF IS CONFIRMED at v2/apps/web/src/components/job-search-view.tsx:70-76 - queryKey ["searches"], enabled: session.data?.authenticated === true, refetchInterval: 5000. An UNCONDITIONAL 5-SECOND POLL OF /api/searches GATED ONLY ON BEING AUTHENTICATED, plus the 10s poll of /api/searches/:id while non-terminal. BOTH NUMBERS MATCH THIS TICKET EXACTLY. Only the app.ts half remains.
REVIEW WINDOW CAVEAT: three sessions were writing concurrently; re-check if a cited file moved between roughly 15:05 and 17:00 IST on 2026-09-25.

THE app.ts HALF IS DONE 2026-09-25: eleven routes carry owner-keyed budgets at app.ts:507-831 - searches-read 240/60, leads-read 240/60, profile-read 120/60, market-read 120/60 - with 429 documented in OpenAPI.

THE BUDGET SIZING REASONING IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING, because it is the difference between a limit and a tripwire: the budgets sit ~20x the MEASURED poll rates (12/min and 6/min) ON PURPOSE - "a budget a normal session can reach is one that gets raised the first time it fires". A limit tuned so tightly that ordinary use trips it does not get respected; it gets relaxed, and then it protects nothing.

COMPLETE AS OF 2026-09-25: ALL FOURTEEN AUTHENTICATED GET ROUTES CARRY A BUDGET - eleven newly via readBudget, plus preparation, export and events which already had their own. VERIFIED BY ENUMERATING EVERY ROUTE, NOT BY SAMPLING. That distinction is the one AC1 actually demands, since a sampled inventory cannot establish "authenticated GET routes carry a proportionate limit" of the routes it did not look at.

THE LAST FIX IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE: /api/searches/:id/events had its rate limit placed AFTER database.getSearch() and the retained-window query, so AN OVER-BUDGET CALLER STILL COST TWO DATABASE QUERIES PER REJECTION - the limiter was protecting the response but not the resource, which is most of the reason to have one. Moved above both, and deliberately BELOW parsing, so malformed input still receives a deterministic 400 rather than a 429 that hides it.

AC3 IS MET BY A TEST THAT CAN ONLY PASS FOR THE RIGHT REASON, which is materially stronger than a test that passes: with the budget exhausted, a request for a NON-EXISTENT run returns 429 INSTEAD OF 404. That outcome is only possible if the limit precedes the lookup, so the assertion observes the ORDERING rather than merely the limit. FALSIFIED BY RESTORING THE OLD ORDER - 404 !== 429. Both the rejected boundary and its falsification are present.
CEILING, RECORDED SO QA IS NOT READ AS DONE: the evidence is local. The chain to a promotion runs through CI, and that hop has not fired. Promotable on a green CI run; not promoted here.

Current Node 24 CI verification: runs 36385161068 and 36385785464 completed green, including the fourteen-route authenticated GET coverage and the rate-limit ordering test. All three acceptance criteria are evidenced; no criterion remains open.

items.title: Resume-derived titles have no character allowlist and flow verbatim into stored match evidence
items.userProblem: A resume-controlled string reaches stored, API-served match evidence without content constraint, so any future non-React render site silently inherits an injection surface.
items.source: Forensic security audit finding M-4, 2026-09-25
acceptanceCriteria: derived.titles is constrained at extraction time in packages/resume/src/derive.ts, matching the discipline already applied to techStack and recentSkills
The constraint is proven with hostile fixtures - markup, control characters, template syntax - that must be rejected or stripped, not merely length-bounded
Existing legitimate titles continue to extract correctly; the constraint must not silently discard real data
evidence: Current Node 24 CI verification: runs 36385161068 and 36385785464 completed green; no acceptance criterion remains open in the ticket record.

AUDIT FINDING M-4: packages/resume/src/derive.ts extracts derived.titles by regex, length-bounded but with NO CHARACTER ALLOWLIST - unlike techStack and recentSkills, which are taxonomy-bound and therefore cannot carry arbitrary content. Orchestrator partially verified: regex-based, non-taxonomy extraction confirmed present in derive.ts (ROLE_WORDS, DATE_STRIP_RE around line 353). The absence of an allowlist is carried forward from the audit and should be confirmed precisely before implementing.

THE PATH: since CS-22 removed collect.ts derived: null override, a resume-derived title flows into candidate.titles, is interpolated VERBATIM into MatchDimensionScore.reason - typed z.string() with no content restriction - and is stored in MatchBreakdown and served over the authenticated API.

NOT EXPLOITABLE TODAY, stated plainly so the priority is not inflated: the only renderer is match-evidence.tsx, which is plain auto-escaping JSX; the auditor found no dangerouslySetInnerHTML anywhere it read; the data is same-owner only; and it is absent from both public export paths.

THE REAL COST is future-facing: any new non-React render site - an email digest, a PDF export, an admin snapshot - would silently inherit an injection surface with no warning, because nothing at the boundary says this string is untrusted. The fix is cheap and belongs at extraction time.
INTERSECTS CS-46 (resume-derived matching facts have no owner approval or per-skill exclusion gate). Coordinate: both concern what resume-derived facts are allowed to become once they reach matching.
FINDING CONFIRMED BY EXECUTION, not by reading - the builder ran deriveTitles on the unmodified file and captured the output: " Senior Engineer" yielded [" Senior Engineer"]; a

FIXED at extraction time inside deriveTitles push(), per segment, so nothing downstream can bypass it. Refuses < > { } $ backtick backslash " = | , C0/C1 controls, DEL, zero-width, bidi, isolates and BOM - CHECKED BY CODE POINT RATHER THAN A REGEX LITERAL, because no-control-regex is a root lint error and the escape hatch is forbidden. Stray characters outside the allowlist are replaced with a space rather than discarding the title. BOTH DIRECTIONS PROVEN ABLE TO FAIL, which is what makes AC3 real: disabling the constraint fails 12 hostile checks while the 10 legitimate-title checks KEEP PASSING - that asymmetry is what shows the hostile checks are doing the work. Making the allowlist over-strict (/[^\p{L} ]/gu) fails 9 real-world-title checks: hyphen, period, ampersand, slash, comma+digit, C++ plus, C# hash, typographic apostrophe. A constraint that silently discards real data would be a worse bug than the one it fixes, and that is now guarded. Root suite 1055 -> 1078 (+23), Orchestrator-verified exit 0. CONSUMER CHAIN: deriveTitles -> deriveFields -> derived.titles -> buildCandidateContext -> MatchDimensionScore.reason -> stored MatchBreakdown -> authenticated API -> match-evidence.tsx (auto-escaping JSX). EVIDENCE STOPS AT deriveFields: no hostile fixture was run end-to-end through parse -> match -> stored evidence. Priority NOT inflated - still not exploitable today. TWO RESIDUALS DISCLOSED: the constraint refuses | outright, which is dead-safe today because the segment splitter consumes | first, but would become load-bearing if the splitter changed; and ROLE_WORDS is English-only so non-English resumes extract no titles at all - pre-existing, unchanged, and worth its own ticket.

RE-REVIEW 2026-09-25: APPROVED WITH FINDINGS, and notably the FIRST falsification claim all night a reviewer could CONFIRM rather than defer on. It recovered the 12/10 split exactly from the file (10 it.each hostile cases + the whole-resume property test + the stray-character test = 12; the legitimate it.each has exactly 10 entries, none containing a refused or stray character, so disabling the constraint leaves all 10 green). Its words: the split being exactly recoverable from the file is itself good evidence the number was measured, not estimated. It rates the whole-resume property test the strongest and says keep it, because a per-code-point assertion over output catches cases nobody enumerated. It credited two things my evidence undersold: the dash-to-pipe rewrite happens BEFORE the split, so the pipe the code itself introduces never reaches the refusal set; and every surviving segment must additionally satisfy ROLE_WORDS.test(part), a substantial second narrowing that materially limits attacker control. F-2 IS NOT A GAP and the reasoning is worth preserving: U+061C, U+2060 and the Tag characters are category Cf, fall outside the allowlist, and TITLE_STRAY_RE neutralises them to a space. The two tiers compose into DEFAULT-DENY - the refusal list decides what KILLS a segment, and everything else unknown is neutralised but survivable. That is what makes the fix durable: the refusal list does not need to be exhaustive to be safe.

F-1 FIXED - the one exception to that default-deny design was an explicit ALLOW, and it let the invisible class back in. TITLE_STRAY_RE permits \p{M} so accents survive, and \p{M} includes Mn, which contains Variation Selectors U+FE00-FE0F, the VS Supplement U+E0100-E01EF and U+180B-180D. Invisible, outside every refusal range, surviving into a stored title - and the doc comment states the intent is to exclude characters used to make a string read as something other than what it is, which is exactly what a variation selector does. Added all three ranges to isRefusedCodePoint in the file existing idiom. PROVEN ABLE TO FAIL: removing the three ranges fails exactly the three new hostile cases (variation selector, Mongolian free variation selector, supplementary variation selector), 3 failed / 52 passed. Reverted, 55/55 green.

F-4 DECIDED AND FIXED, not left undecided - this was the over-strict failure mode the brief specifically warned about, and it was live. A refused character costs the ENTIRE segment, and nine of the ten refusals have effectively zero probability in a real title, but "$" does not: "Engineer, $1B Platform segment" was being dropped SILENTLY. DECISION: strip rather than refuse. "$" moved out of TITLE_REFUSED_SYNTAX and now falls through to TITLE_STRAY_RE, neutralised to a space, title kept. Refusing it was also REDUNDANT, which settled the call: template interpolation needs "${", and "{" is still refused, so "${...}" still costs the segment. BOTH HALVES PROVEN: reinstating "$" in the refusal set fails the new "keeps a real title carrying a currency symbol" test (1 failed / 54 passed); and a new test asserts "Engineer ${constructor.constructor(1)}" still yields [], so the composition is asserted rather than assumed. Reverted, 55/55 green. Root suite 1078 -> 1083, exit 0, Orchestrator-verified. HONEST PROCESS NOTE: my first attempt at this falsification silently failed to apply its edit and the suite passed - I caught that the Set was unchanged and redid it properly rather than reporting a green run as a falsification. A falsification that did not actually mutate anything is worse than none.

F-3 SETTLED WITH A SHELL, which the reviewer could not do, and the answer is the unfavourable one. The load-bearing unknown was the server Zod schema for owner-typed preferences.titles. It is packages/shared/src/schemas.ts:30 - titles: z.array(z.string().trim().min(1)).min(1).max(25). NO CHARACTER CONSTRAINT: trim and non-empty only, capped at 25 entries. So the owner-typed inlet into candidate.titles is genuinely unconstrained, and this fix closes ONE of TWO inlets. SCOPE DECISION, recorded rather than glossed: AC1 is written about derived.titles, so this ticket criteria are met and the owner-typed inlet is intentionally excluded by this ticket's derived-title criterion. The reasoning for treating it separately is a different threat model - the resume inlet accepts a crafted file, whereas the typed inlet is the single owner typing into their own workspace and rendering it back to themselves. That is self-inflicted, not attacker-controlled. BUT THE RATIONALE IS NOT FULLY ELIMINATED, and I will not claim it is: a future email digest, PDF export or admin snapshot renders MatchDimensionScore.reason regardless of which inlet the title came from. The durable fix is to constrain at the reason boundary rather than per-inlet. That is deliberately NOT done here - it belongs with CS-46, which already owns what resume-derived facts may become - and it needs its own ticket if the owner wants the typed inlet covered too.

BOTH FINDINGS CLOSED, AND A RELAYED DESCRIPTION OF THE FIX WAS WRONG - corrected here at source. F-56-1 was reported as fixed by `expect(readable.titles.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)`. IT IS NOT. The actual assertion at derive.test.ts:232 is `expect(titles).toContain("Principal Platform Engineer")`, under a comment at :226 beginning "F-56-1 (re-review 2026-09-25): THIS ASSERTION IS THE TEST".

THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS AND IS RECORDED SO NOBODY LATER "SIMPLIFIES" IT BACK: a length check passes if ANY title survives, which is satisfied by an implementation that mangles the expected title and returns something else. toContain proves THE SPECIFIC EXPECTED TITLE survived. The delivered fix is MORE rigorous than the one described, not less.

HOW THE MISREPORT HAPPENED IS THE INSTRUCTIVE PART: a grep for `titles.length` hit a DIFFERENT assertion in a DIFFERENT test and was reported as the F-56-1 fix WITHOUT READING THE SURROUNDING LINES. That is searching for a pattern and then offering the pattern you searched for as evidence - the third instance tonight of the hazard already recorded in AGENT-SETUP.md, that this codebase documents its reasoning inline and quotes the identifiers someone would later grep for. The line that should have been found carries a five-line comment explaining the vacuity, and was there to be read.

The distinction is not cosmetic: "ALL THREE CRITERIA MET" IS FALSIFIABLE BY COUNTING; "ALL APPLICABLE CRITERIA MET" CANNOT FAIL, because an unmet criterion can be reclassified as not-applicable without anyone editing a number. It is the same shape as \bsurfaced\b, DEFERRED and eol=crlf - a word anyone can write that silently changes how a claim is graded - except that this one sat in the STATUS FIELD OF TEN TICKETS, which is the field a promotion decision reads. That makes it the most consequential of the four, not the least.

Two of the ten were then found wrong within minutes - CS-74 (AC3 half-met) and CS-52 (AC4 unmet) - so the remaining eight cannot be assumed right. A COUNTED CLAIM OVER AN UNCOUNTED CRITERION IS NO BETTER THAN THE HEDGE IT REPLACED; it is only more falsifiable, and falsifying it is the outstanding work.

items.title: POST /api/logout non-null-asserts a session cookie the request hook does not guarantee
items.userProblem: An auth-adjacent route carries an unjustified non-null assertion that can only ever turn a missing cookie into a 500.
items.source: Forensic security audit LOW finding, 2026-09-25 - VERIFIED by the Orchestrator
acceptanceCriteria: POST /api/logout handles a missing session cookie without a non-null assertion and without a 500
A logout with no cookie returns the same safe, non-enumerating response as a normal logout
A test covers the missing-cookie path and is proven able to fail
evidence: Current Node 24 CI verification: runs 36385161068 and 36385785464 completed green; no acceptance criterion remains open in the ticket record.

VERIFIED BY THE ORCHESTRATOR 2026-09-25 against current bytes. v2/apps/api/src/app.ts line 249, inside app.post(/api/logout) declared at line 248: "await auth.logout(request.cookies[sessionCookie]!);" - a non-null assertion on a value the onRequest hook does not guarantee exists on this path.

Worst case is a 500 rather than any security failure, so the severity is genuinely LOW. It is recorded because an unjustified non-null assertion in an auth-adjacent route is exactly the kind of thing that stops being harmless when the surrounding code changes, and because the engineering contract forbids using a type escape hatch to hide a real nullability question.

FIXED 2026-09-25, and the cold criteria read changed the scope - this was NOT the one-line fix the ticket predicted. AC1 was the easy half: app.ts now reads the cookie into a const and calls auth.logout only when it is defined; the non-null assertion is gone. AC2 ("a logout with no cookie returns the SAME safe, non-enumerating response as a normal logout") required more. The onRequest hook at app.ts:118-122 returned 401 BEFORE the handler whenever there was no session, so the handler was unreachable with a missing cookie and a no-cookie logout answered 401 - which is not the same response as a normal logout, and is mildly enumerating. A narrow exemption was added: no session AND path === /api/logout returns early. SECURITY REASONING, recorded because this is an auth-path change: ONLY /api/logout is exempt and ONLY when there is no session. Origin is still matched above that line. CSRF is still enforced whenever a session exists - asserted directly (a forged request with a live session returns 403). With no session there is nothing to revoke, so the exemption grants no capability. trustProxy, security headers, rate limits and Argon2id are untouched. OpenAPI needed no change and now matches reality better, since POST /api/logout documents only 200/500.

PROVEN ABLE TO FAIL IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which matters because the two halves of the fix are independent: restoring the non-null assertion (keeping the hook exemption) fails with actual 500 vs expected 200; removing the hook exemption (keeping the handler guard) fails with actual 401 vs expected 200. So neither half is decorative. Both reverted, green after. The test asserts that no-cookie, stale-cookie and live-session logouts return IDENTICAL status AND identical body. ORCHESTRATOR-VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY, and this mattered here: the builder could not run test:ui (Orchestrator-owned). I ran it after its changes - exit 0 on chromium, firefox and webkit, and that suite exercises the real sign-out journey through the shared topbar. An auth-hook change that passed unit and integration but broke the actual sign-out path would have been caught there. CONSUMER CHAIN: app.ts /api/logout <- authenticated-shell.tsx:69 is the ONLY caller <- rendered by every (app) route <- exercised by check-ui.ts <- test:ui <- ci.yml. The last hop is WIRED, NOT CI-EXECUTED.

SECURITY REVIEW 2026-09-25 (read-only, no shell and no execute - it said so up front and marked execution-dependent claims UNCONFIRMED). VERDICT: APPROVED WITH FINDINGS, does not block UAT. Q1 (can any other path reach the exemption?) BYPASS NOT POSSIBLE - and it found a BETTER reason than the one I gave. The compared value is request.routeOptions.url, which in Fastify 5 is the REGISTERED ROUTE PATTERN, not the request line. Routing completes before the first onRequest hook. So every normalisation shape I asked about (trailing slash, case, %74 encoding, /api/./logout, //api/logout, dot-segments, query strings) has only two outcomes: it matches the POST route, in which case the exemption and the dispatch agree BY DEFINITION and there is no divergence to exploit; or it does not match, routeOptions.url is undefined, and the 401 fires. The whole normalisation-mismatch class is structurally unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely. It also verified /api/logout is registered exactly once. Q2 (byte-identical, or merely both 200?) BYTE-IDENTICAL CONFIRMED for status, body and headers. clearCookie is called UNCONDITIONALLY outside the if with a constant options object, so the Set-Cookie is emitted identically either way; the body is a fixed literal through a fixed response schema, so Content-Length matches. On timing it traced the DB round trips and found the security-relevant comparison - valid token vs well-formed-but-invalid - is TWO QUERIES EITHER WAY. It also found a genuine distinguisher I had not noted: with a live session the request does NOT take the exemption and hits CSRF, so POST /api/logout with no x-csrf-token returns 403 for a live cookie and 200 for a dead one - a validity oracle. It rated this P3 because GET /api/session already returns authenticated true/false for any cookie with NO CSRF and NO Origin requirement, a cheaper pre-existing oracle of the same information, and because the change did not introduce it.

P3 METHOD-QUALIFICATION FIXED. The exemption matched on path alone. Inert today since only POST is registered, but a real trapdoor: a future app.get(/api/logout) - the obvious way someone adds a plain sign-out link - would have inherited anonymity AND skipped the Origin check, which excludes GET. Now gated on request.method === POST. Two regression tests added: GET /api/logout must still answer 401, and a neighbouring path must still answer 401. P3 OPENAPI FIXED, AND MY OWN EVIDENCE WAS WRONG IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION. I had recorded that the document "now matches reality better". FALSE. The literal in documentation does say 200/500, but registerOpenApi transform augments it: it added response[401] and security [{session, csrf}] for every URL not in an anonymous allowlist, and /api/logout was not in that list - so the published document claimed logout could 401 (no longer reachable) and required a session plus CSRF (no longer true). Added /api/logout to the anonymous array. It remains a mutation so 403 and 413 are still documented, which is correct because a caller WITH a live session does still fail CSRF. REVIEWER P2 "no automated coverage" REFUTED WITH EVIDENCE, and the reviewer flagged its own uncertainty honestly ("NOT LOCATED - UNCONFIRMED, not disproven"). The CS-57 regression test exists at v2/packages/core/src/database.test.ts:3714 and the CSRF-403 assertion it could not find is at :3771-3777 (const forged = await app.inject(...); assert.equal(forged.statusCode, 403)). It runs in test:integration. It was looking in check-ui.ts and had no grep. ITS UNDERLYING OBSERVATION STANDS THOUGH: there is NO test file anywhere under v2/apps/api, so API HTTP-level tests live in packages/core/src/database.test.ts, which is not where anyone would look for them.

P2 RATE LIMIT: IMPLEMENTED, THEN DELIBERATELY REVERTED. THIS IS A HARD STOP, NOT A SKIPPED FINDING. The reviewer is right that exempting logout made it the only unauthenticated WRITE path (a SELECT plus a DELETE per call). I implemented logout:<sha256(request.ip)> at 30/60 following the exact pattern already used by login and register at app.ts:237/246. IT BROKE A REAL PROPERTY TEST: database.test.ts:3300 deliberately exhausts the LOGIN limiter and then asserts logout still returns 200 - being locked out of signing IN must not lock you out of signing OUT. My limiter turned that into 429 !== 200, reproducibly, with failureType testCodeFailure (NOT the CS-58 cross-talk signature, which is uncaughtException plus "terminating connection due to administrator command"). I checked that distinction specifically rather than assuming it was the known flake. I DID NOT RAISE THE NUMBER TO MAKE IT PASS. That would be tuning to green rather than designing a control, and the investigation found a real design problem underneath: trustProxy: false correctly makes request.ip the real peer, but the deployed topology puts Caddy in front of the API, so EVERY request arrives from one address and a per-IP limit is effectively a GLOBAL limit. The same weakness applies to the existing login/register limiters, which is a separate pre-existing finding. Reverted; test:integration 43/43 exit 0. The finding remains OPEN and is re-ticketed rather than lost. The reviewer explicitly rated this P2 as NOT blocking UAT.

RUNTIME CAVEAT ADDED 2026-09-25 TO EVERY RESULT RECORDED TODAY: all local verification in this run was executed on Node v22.23.2, while package.json requires >=24.0.0, .nvmrc says 24 and CI uses 24. This does not invalidate the passes, but it RECLASSIFIES them - each was obtained on a runtime the project does not support, and any could differ on Node 24. Applies to typecheck, lint, test:unit, deploy:gate:test, eol:check and the three-engine test:ui runs alike.

STANDARD WORDING ADOPTED 2026-09-25 from CS-39, which stated the claim, its ceiling and its unlock in one line: "All three criteria met and asserted. Promotable on a green CI run; not promoted here." Every ticket in this cohort now carries the same sentence, plus the second bar discovered later - local execution on Node v22.23.2 against a declared floor of 24. NO QA TICKET IS PROMOTABLE TONIGHT ON EXECUTION EVIDENCE, and that is ONE GATE rather than nineteen separate problems.

CONFIRMED CLEAN 2026-09-25: no acceptance criterion is contradicted by this tickets own evidence. CS-57 is QA, P3, three criteria, and its currentStep carries the CS-39 template correctly with BOTH standing caveats attached - not CI-executed, and locally executed on Node v22.23.2 against a floor of 24. ADD IT TO THE SAME COHORT AS CS-35, CS-39, CS-56, CS-63 AND CS-67: blocked on CI execution alone.

AND RECORD THE REVIEWERS REFUSAL AS CORRECT BEHAVIOUR RATHER THAN AS A GAP. Three probes failed to locate the ticket because the file had reordered, and it declined to answer from its earlier-batch memory: "that read was ~15:10 and the ticket has moved and been edited since. Giving you a stale verdict dressed as a current one is the error I have been flagging all night." IN A TREE THREE SESSIONS ARE WRITING, A REMEMBERED READ IS NOT A CURRENT READ, and saying so is a better outcome than a confident answer.

WORDING CORRECTED 2026-09-25 FROM "All applicable criteria met" TO THE COUNTED FORM. The distinction is not cosmetic: "ALL THREE CRITERIA MET" IS FALSIFIABLE BY COUNTING; "ALL APPLICABLE CRITERIA MET" CANNOT FAIL, because an unmet criterion can be reclassified as not-applicable without anyone editing a number. It is the same shape as \bsurfaced\b, DEFERRED and eol=crlf - a word anyone can write that silently changes how a claim is graded - except that this one sat in the STATUS FIELD OF TEN TICKETS, which is the field a promotion decision reads. That makes it the most consequential of the four, not the least.

COUNT NOT YET RE-TAKEN 2026-09-25, recorded as owed work rather than left as an unverified claim. When "All applicable criteria met" was replaced with the counted form across ten tickets, THE WORDING WAS CORRECTED AND THE COUNT WAS NOT. Two of the ten were then found wrong within minutes - CS-74 (AC3 half-met) and CS-52 (AC4 unmet) - so the remaining eight cannot be assumed right. A COUNTED CLAIM OVER AN UNCOUNTED CRITERION IS NO BETTER THAN THE HEDGE IT REPLACED; it is only more falsifiable, and falsifying it is the outstanding work.

TOKEN SCAN 2026-09-25 RETURNED CLEAN FOR THIS TICKET - every criterion is named by identifier somewhere in the evidence. RECORDED AT ITS REAL STRENGTH AND NO HIGHER: THAT MEANS "NO CRITERION IS UNMENTIONED", NOT "ALL CRITERIA ARE MET". The COUNT NOT YET RE-TAKEN label STAYS, because a proxy that asks whether the token AC2 appears is not asking whether AC2 is satisfied. Nothing suggests a problem here; nothing has verified one either.

AC1 VERIFIED AT SOURCE 2026-09-25 - "POST /api/logout handles a missing session cookie without a non-null assertion." The onRequest hook reads: if (!session && request.method === "POST" && path === "/api/logout") return; then if (!session) throw new HttpError(401). NO NON-NULL ASSERTION; the anonymous POST returns early and everything else without a session gets 401. MET.

AND THE request.method === "POST" TERM IS A GUARD AGAINST A CHANGE NOBODY HAS MADE YET, with its reasoning recorded in place at app.ts:133-137: only POST is registered today so matching the path alone was INERT - "but it was a trapdoor: a future app.get('/api/logout'), THE OBVIOUS WAY SOMEONE WOULD ADD A PLAIN SIGN-OUT LINK, would silently inherit anonymity AND SKIP THE ORIGIN CHECK ABOVE, WHICH EXCLUDES GET. The method term costs nothing and removes that."

RECORD THAT AS AN EXAMPLE TO COPY, because it is cheap and almost nobody writes it: THE GUARD EXISTS BECAUSE THE OBVIOUS FUTURE IMPLEMENTATION WOULD HAVE BEEN THE DANGEROUS ONE. Same instinct as the two-migrations split and the origin exclusion - MAKE THE WRONG FUTURE EDIT FAIL RATHER THAN TRUSTING IT NOT TO HAPPEN. An inert condition that closes a trapdoor is not dead code.

PROVISIONAL MARKING WITHDRAWN 2026-09-25, SAME DAY IT WAS APPLIED, BECAUSE IT WAS TOO BROAD AND THE WITHDRAWAL IS RECORDED RATHER THAN SILENT. The #19 finding was real - tsc -b exited 0 with a production type error - BUT IT WAS OVERSTATED AS "the gate could not fail". THE GATE COULD FAIL; ONLY ITS FIRST LINK COULD NOT. `npm run typecheck` chains four commands and the last, check-test-types.mjs, filters on /^\S+\.ts\(\d+,\d+\): error TS\d+/ - WHICH MATCHES A PRODUCTION FILE AS READILY AS A TEST FILE - and exits 1. Anyone running the npm script WOULD have been told.

items.title: Two unexplained intermittent test failures with no ticket and no owner
items.userProblem: A suite that fails roughly one run in three teaches everyone to re-run it, which is how a real regression gets waved through as "just the flake".
items.source: Observed directly by the Orchestrator across many runs on 2026-09-24/25; owed as a ticket per owner instruction
acceptanceCriteria: Each of the two flakes is either root-caused and fixed, or reproduced deterministically and documented with the precise trigger - not merely re-run until green
No assertion is weakened, no timeout is inflated and no retry is added to make either disappear
docs/KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md reflects the outcome, including any part that remains unexplained
evidence: FLAKE 1 - WebKit click stability in check-ui.ts. Observed 2026-09-25: "locator.click: Timeout 30000ms exceeded ... waiting for getByRole(button, {name: Back to Search}) - locator resolved to <button type="button"> - attempting click action - waiting for element to be visible, enabled and stable" at check-ui.ts:951. The locator RESOLVED; the element never settled. WebKit only, roughly one run in three to one in five. The immediately following run was green on all three engines. Notably it surfaced during the WCAG 2.2 enablement run and was initially easy to mistake for a 2.2 violation - it is not; no axe violation was reported.

FLAKE 2 - v2 test:integration on a quiet database. Mostly explained: concurrent agents creating and dropping test_<uuid> databases on one PostgreSQL instance, where DROP DATABASE terminates other backends, producing failureType uncaughtException and "terminating connection due to administrator command" in pg-protocol, with a DIFFERENT test failing each run. That is genuine cross-talk and not a product defect. BUT it also failed once (41/42) on a demonstrably QUIET database with no concurrent agent running, then passed 42/42 immediately after. The failing test identity was NOT captured on that specific run - a real evidence gap, recorded rather than glossed. market.test.ts is the strongest candidate.

THIS IS NOT A NEW PROBLEM, AND THAT IS THE POINT: docs/KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md has carried "One intermittent test failure is unexplained" for some time, saying of a never-identified second test file "It has not recurred, but has not recurred is not fixed." It has now recurred. The section was updated on 2026-09-24 with the new evidence and the named candidate, but nothing owned the work until this ticket.

WHY P2 AND NOT LOWER: an intermittent suite is corrosive to every other ticket in this backlog. Three checks-that-cannot-fail were found tonight; the defence against a fourth is that a red run is believed. A suite that cries wolf destroys exactly that.

NEW REPRODUCTION 2026-09-25 (CS-13 re-review cycle): check-ui.ts:2301 `await quiet("cs-13 error state " + width)` timed out on FIREFOX at 768px with "never stopped issuing requests", then passed on an immediate re-run with no code change between the two runs. Third distinct intermittent in this suite alongside the WebKit click-stability timeout and the integration failure surviving a quiet DB. Same underlying shape as the documented problem that a page polling on an interval can never satisfy a network-idle wait. Consequence for gating: a single green run of check-ui.ts is not sufficient evidence of stability, and CI wiring this suite without a retry or a deflake will produce failures unrelated to the change under test.

NOT ATTEMPTABLE TONIGHT, recorded as a deferral with its reason rather than left looking available. AC1 requires each flake to be root-caused, and flake 2s recorded dominant cause is "concurrent agents creating and dropping test_<uuid> databases on one PostgreSQL instance" - WHICH IS THE CURRENT OPERATING MODE. Three sessions are running concurrently against one instance, so any attempt tonight would be measuring the condition it is supposed to eliminate. Defer to a single-writer window.
REVIEW WINDOW CAVEAT: three sessions were writing concurrently; re-check if a cited file moved between roughly 15:05 and 16:45 IST on 2026-09-25.

POSSIBLE CONTRIBUTING CAUSE ADDED 2026-09-25, marked as a hypothesis not a diagnosis: every recorded flake in this ticket was observed on Node v22.23.2, two major versions below the projects declared floor of >=24. That does not explain any specific flake and must not be treated as one, but AC1 requires each flake root-caused, and "root-caused on an unsupported runtime" is not a root cause. Re-observe on Node 24 before concluding anything.

FOURTH INTERMITTENT RECORDED 2026-09-25, AND IT IS IN v2 test:unit - THE SUITE BEING CITED AS 55/55 IN THE INTEGRATION PASS. Observed directly in this session: one run returned 53 pass / 2 FAIL / exit 1. An immediately preceding and an immediately following run both returned 55 pass / 0 fail / exit 0, as did two runs from the coordinating session. SO THE SUITE PASSES ABOUT THREE TIMES IN FOUR.

LIMITATION STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: the failing test names were NOT captured - the output filter used at the time did not match the failure lines, and the next run was green so there was nothing left to read. WHAT IS ESTABLISHED IS THE FACT OF INTERMITTENCY, NOT ITS LOCATION. Anyone reproducing it should capture the whole log, not a filtered view.

A PLAUSIBLE CAUSE, MARKED AS INFERENCE AND NOT ASSERTED: the AI provider tests in this suite exercise real network behaviour - the run log carries genuine 401, 402, 429, 500 and 503 responses plus an eight-second timeout case - and timing-sensitive network tests are the usual source of this pattern. That is a hypothesis; it has not been confirmed and must not be recorded as the cause.

CONSEQUENCE FOR HOW THE INTEGRATION PASS IS CITED, which matters more than the flake itself: "55/55" IS NOT A STABLE RESULT, IT IS THE COMMON RESULT. A gate that fails one run in four is not a gate yet. Cite the pass with this attached, or the number implies a stability nobody has measured.

Run 36339115982 captured the V2 cross-talk precisely: bull-queue.test.ts and the password-change database test failed together while test files shared one PostgreSQL service; the latter received 'terminating connection due to administrator command'. test:integration now serializes its nine service-backed files while retaining every assertion.

Run 36339477079 captured the root browser failure rather than retrying it: Chromium at 320px had headerOverlap=true on /leads while Firefox and WebKit did not. The wordmark is now hidden below 360px, retaining the labelled compass link and the 40px theme and profile controls without overlap.

2026-09-28 local Node 24.19.0 verification after the responsive correction: root typecheck and production build pass; test:ui passes on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit with overflow=false and headerOverlap=false at 320/390/768/1024/1440px, plus the four additional 320px routes.

Runs 36355556149 and 36355820525 reproduce the quiet-database case with file concurrency already fixed at one. The first attributed 'terminating connection due to administrator command' to the password-change case. Removing FORCE from that case made the next run identify the source precisely: the partial-search test generated asynchronous activity after it ended, and its own DROP DATABASE WITH (FORCE) terminated that client, replacing the cleanup boundary with an uncaught exception. Every database.test.ts teardown now uses ordinary DROP after pool.end(); this is stricter, not a retry, because a surviving client must produce an explicit ownership failure instead of being killed. CI verification is pending.

2026-09-28: hosted workflow run https://github.com/varunjakkampudi-tech/careerscope/actions/runs/36424073277 passed the serialized V2 integration and all three browser engines after the teardown and narrow-layout corrections; no retry or timeout inflation was introduced.
